Field studies on Gould (Catharus dryas) in the montane cloud forests of Central America have yielded detailed life-history data under controlled ambient temperatures. Neonates emerge from their nests with a remarkably low wet weight at birth of 3.89 grams [Wwb = 3.89 grams], a mass that reflects the altricial development strategy typical of many thrushes. Incubation experiments conducted at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] demonstrate that hatching occurs after approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days], a relatively brief embryonic period that may be linked to the reduced yolk investment implied by the small hatchling mass. This abbreviated incubation phase likely allows females to initiate subsequent nesting attempts more rapidly within a single breeding season, a critical advantage in the unpredictable highland environments this species occupies.

Under the thermal conditions characteristic of active metabolic periods in this thrush, specifically 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones governs post-hatching ontogeny. The fledgling stage, marked by the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching], a rapid transition that minimizes exposure to nest predation at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Following departure from the nest, the growing juvenile enters a period of intense physiological development before reaching gonadal maturation; puberty is attained at 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively swift transition to sexual maturity is notable among Neotropical thrushes and may be an adaptation to the short, seasonal windows of food abundance in these high-elevation habitats.

Female Gould attain an ultimate wet weight of 30 grams [Wwi = 30 grams], a modest adult body mass that aligns with the species' affiliation with the smaller-bodied members of the genus Catharus. This asymptotic size is reached gradually over the first year of life, with growth rates constrained by the energetic demands of flight and thermoregulation in the cool, humid cloud forest environment. The maximum lifespan recorded for wild individuals in the thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], a longevity that is intermediate among passerines of comparable mass and that may be influenced by the reduced predation pressure found in their remote montane refugia. Senescence-related mortality becomes apparent after the seventh or eighth year.

Reproductive investment in this species is characterized by a conservative annual strategy. Females produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], wherein each clutch contains 2 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch contains 2 eggs]. This modest reproductive output is coupled with an extended period of biparental care, which together suggest a life-history strategy oriented toward offspring quality rather than numerical quantity. The time since birth at first brood, representing the age at which a female successfully fledges her first clutch, is 365 days [tR = 365 days] when incubated at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay reflects the substantial somatic investment required to reach adult body size before allocating resources to egg production and nesting behavior.

Comparative analyses within the genus Catharus reveal that Gould exhibits a somewhat accelerated life history relative to its higher-latitude congeners. Whereas many northern thrushes delay first reproduction into their second calendar year, the montane environment permits a shorter interval between hatching and first successful breeding. The species' reproductive rate, expressed as a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] of 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch], results in a relatively low annual fecundity that is consistent with the stable, low-predation environments of tropical montane forests. Furthermore, the combination of rapid juvenile development and extended adult longevity—approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] in the wild—positions this species along the slower end of the passerine life-history continuum, emphasizing survival and repeated, modest reproductive efforts over a protracted adult lifespan at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].
